raw_text:
### Introduction and Pathophysiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium [1]. While over 30 proteins can form amyloid, the vast majority of clinical cases are driven by two precursor proteins: monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL amyloidosis) and transthyretin (ATTR amyloidosis) [1,2]. AL amyloidosis is a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia wherein unstable light chains misfold into beta-pleated sheets, causing rapid myocardial damage and severe systemic dysfunction [3,4]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis stems from the dissociation of the hepatic-derived transthyretin homotetramer into unstable monomers [1,2]. ATTR is further subclassified into wild-type (ATTRwt)—predominantly affecting older male patients—and hereditary or mutant (ATTRm), which is caused by pathogenic variants in the *TTR* gene [2,5].

### Clinical Presentation and Red Flags
Historically, CA was considered a rare, untreatable condition [6,7]. However, epidemiologic and imaging advancements have revealed that it is a frequent, underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [8,9]. Up to 13% of patients hospitalized with HFpEF and up to 16% of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis harbor occult ATTRwt [10]. Recognizing clinical "red flags" is crucial for early detection [11,12]. These include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, low-voltage electrocardiograms in the presence of echocardiographic left ventricular hypertrophy, and unexplained conduction system disease [1,12].

### Diagnostic Evaluation
The diagnostic landscape has undergone a paradigm shift, largely replacing routine endomyocardial biopsy with a highly accurate non-invasive algorithm [3,10]. Initial evaluation of suspected CA relies on speckle-tracking echocardiography, which classically demonstrates an apical sparing pattern of longitudinal strain [13]. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides excellent tissue characterization, revealing diffuse late gadolinium enhancement and markedly elevated native T1 values and extracellular volume fractions [14,15].

To confirm the diagnosis and differentiate between AL and ATTR, a dual-pathway screening approach is mandatory [3,10,16]. First, monoclonal proteins must be ruled out using serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis along with a serum free light chain (FLC) assay [17,18]. Second, technetium-99m pyrophosphate (99mTc-PYP), 3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylate (99mTc-DPD), or hydroxymethylene diphosphonate (99mTc-HMDP) scintigraphy is performed [3,19]. In the absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia (normal FLC and negative immunofixation), a Grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake on bone scintigraphy is 100% specific for ATTR cardiomyopathy, obviating the need for biopsy [3]. However, if any monoclonal protein is detected, or if scintigraphy is equivocal, an endomyocardial or fat pad biopsy stained with Congo red—revealing apple-green birefringence under polarized light—remains essential to prevent catastrophic misdiagnosis [1,10]. Genetic testing of the *TTR* gene is always required upon diagnosing ATTR to differentiate ATTRwt from ATTRm and guide family screening [12,20].

### Prognostication and Treatment Strategies
The prognosis of CA depends heavily on the subtype and the stage at diagnosis [6,21,22]. The stage in AL amyloidosis is determined using cardiac biomarkers, namely N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and troponins [21]. Treatment of AL amyloidosis is a hematologic emergency focused on rapidly suppressing the clone [17,23]. The current standard of care for newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis is the combination of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone (CyBorD), which has significantly improved hematologic and organ response rates [24,25]. Selected patients may also undergo autologous stem cell transplantation [23].

For ATTR cardiomyopathy, therapeutic strategies aim to either reduce TTR production or stabilize the circulating tetramer [12,26]. Tafamidis, a small-molecule TTR stabilizer, was shown in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial to significantly reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations, while preserving functional capacity [2]. Gene-silencing therapeutics, including the small interfering RNA (siRNA) patisiran and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen, knock down hepatic production of both mutant and wild-type TTR, showing profound benefits in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy and emerging efficacy in cardiomyopathy [27,28,29]. Supportive cardiac care requires careful management: loop diuretics are the mainstay for fluid balance, whereas standard heart failure agents like beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and digoxin are often poorly tolerated or contraindicated due to the restrictive physiology and risk of toxicity [12,18].

### Conclusion
Cardiac amyloidosis is an increasingly recognized etiology of heart failure [1,30]. Early non-invasive diagnosis through multi-modality imaging and rapid screening for monoclonal light chains is paramount [3,16]. With highly effective disease-modifying therapies now available for both AL and ATTR, timely diagnosis directly translates into improved survival and enhanced quality of life for these patients [2,12,24].
